description: BV Labs is a team of four, Zehra Dizlek, Yasemin Yılmaz, Aslı Nur Demirkol and Ayşe Cengiz, working on the Field Shift challenge. We combine software development, data analysis and an interest in sustainable agriculture. Our project, WAGRO, uses NASA Earth observation data to help farmers choose crop rotations that protect soil and save water, with explainable rules, statistics, unsupervised machine learning and optimization.
summary: WAGRO is a prototype decision-support web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect soil and save water. A farmer marks the field on a map and answers four short questions: recent crops, soil and irrigation, priorities, and practical limits. WAGRO then reads NASA Earth observation data for the area around the field: NASA POWER weather and soil wetness, MODIS plant cover, SMAP soil moisture, land surface temperature, GRACE water storage, and elevation. It compares the farmer’s current rotation with alternatives on eight transparent criteria, including water use, nitrogen, organic matter, erosion and climate fit, and searches every allowed rotation for the best balance. Statistics show local climate trends and dry or wet years, and an unsupervised Isolation Forest flags recent months that were unusual for that location. This matters because repeated cereals, bare soil and a shifting climate threaten soil and water, and farmers rarely have easy access to this data. Every result explains why, what is uncertain, and what to check locally.
details:
What it does and how it works:

WAGRO turns a farmer’s answers and NASA data into a short list of crop rotations with reasons. The workflow has three steps. (1) A four-step form records the field location, current and past crops, soil type, pH and irrigation, priorities (water efficiency, soil health, nitrogen, crop diversity, erosion control, income, animal feed) and limits (crops the farmer can sell, row-planter access, cover crops). (2) The app loads 10 years of daily NASA POWER data and computes a water balance with FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration, frost dates, hot days and root-zone soil wetness. Thirty years of monthly data feed the anomaly detection. NASA GIBS maps show MODIS NDVI, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS land surface temperature and GRACE water storage, and a three-year NDVI series is read from the tiles. Elevation tiles give slope and frost-prone low spots. (3) Five options are scored from 0 to 100 on eight criteria: the current rotation, three rule-based alternatives, and the best balance found by an exhaustive Pareto search over every allowed rotation. A three-year timeline shows when soil is bare, and what-if sliders (up to +3 °C, −30% rain) re-score everything.

Methods, kept separate and labelled. Rule-based scoring; optimization (Pareto search); statistics (Mann-Kendall trend test, Sen’s slope, k-means grouping of dry, normal and wet years, NDVI season timing); and unsupervised machine learning (an Isolation Forest on 7 monthly variables over 30 years). In tests with planted anomalies, the Isolation Forest found 34 of 50 moderate multi-variable anomalies, against 2 of 50 for a simple threshold rule. No supervised yield model is claimed.

Benefits and intended impact:

Plain-language guidance that farmers and advisers can check: why each rotation, what it is good for, what is unknown, and what to verify locally. The aim is less bare soil, better nitrogen and water use, and rotations that hold up in dry years. WAGRO supports local advice; it does not replace it.

Tools:

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Leaflet, Zod and Vitest (107 automated tests plus a reproducible evaluation script). Data comes from NASA POWER, NASA GIBS (MODIS, SMAP, GRACE), AWS Terrain Tiles (SRTM / EU-DEM) and OpenStreetMap. There is no database and no API keys; the farmer’s answers stay in their browser.

Creativity:

NDVI values are decoded directly from NASA GIBS map tiles through the published colormap. The Isolation Forest is dependency-free and fitted in the browser for each location. Climate stress tests re-score every option, and every result carries a method label.

Factors we considered:

Data resolution (weather describes about 50 km, not the field). Honesty about uncertainty: crop values are prototype estimates that still need agronomist review, and NDVI cannot identify crops. Farmer-friendly design, privacy, free and open data only, and southern-hemisphere and hot-climate behaviour, which we tested for the Western Cape and the Sahel.
